title: The SR Latch: Two Gates That Remember
quickIdea: Two cross-coupled NOR gates (or two cross-coupled NAND gates) store one bit with no clock. One input sets it, the other resets it, and the combination that asserts both is forbidden.
remember: NOR latch, active-high inputs: S = 1, R = 0 sets Q to 1; S = 0, R = 1 resets Q to 0; S = R = 0 holds; S = R = 1 is forbidden.
NAND latch, active-low inputs: S' = 0 sets; R' = 0 resets; both 1 holds; both 0 is forbidden. The table is the mirror image of the NOR one, so check which gate the question draws.
Characteristic equation of the NOR latch: Q+ = S + R'Q, valid only while S and R are not both 1. With S = R = 1 the equation would say Q+ = 1, which contradicts the hardware.
Why the forbidden input is forbidden: on the NOR latch it forces Q = Q' = 0, so the two outputs stop being complements; on the NAND latch it forces Q = Q' = 1.
The forbidden input is not just an error state, it is a timing hazard. Releasing both inputs at once makes the stored value depend on which gate is faster, so the next state is unpredictable.
The latch is level-sensitive and clockless. That is what separates it from a flip-flop.

example.prompt: A NOR SR latch starts with Q = 0. The inputs go (S, R) = (1, 0), then (0, 0), then (0, 1), then (0, 0). What is Q after each step?
example.work: (1, 0) sets: Q = 1. (0, 0) holds: Q stays 1. (0, 1) resets: Q = 0. (0, 0) holds again: Q stays 0. Each (0, 0) step copies the previous value, which is the memory.
example.answer: Q = 1, 1, 0, 0. Every (0, 0) row of the table is the whole point of the circuit.

gateAngle: GATE hands you a drawn latch and asks for the outputs, or asks whether a given input sequence is legal. The marks are in knowing which polarity the drawn gates use and what the forbidden row does to the outputs.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: A NAND SR latch has inputs S' = 1 and R' = 1. What is Q, and why can it not be read off the gates alone?
variations.answer: Q keeps whatever it held. Both NAND gates see a 1 on their control input, so each output equals the complement of the other output, and the pair settles in whichever of the two stable states it was already in.
variations.why: This is bistability: two consistent solutions exist for the same inputs, and the circuit remembers which one it is in. That is exactly what a memory element is.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Both inputs of a NOR SR latch are pulsed to 1 and released to 0 at exactly the same instant. What can be said about Q?
variations.answer: Nothing definite. The two gates race, and Q settles to whichever gate wins; the value may also be metastable for a short time.
variations.why: This is the reason the row is called forbidden rather than merely illegal. GATE has asked which input combination leaves the output indeterminate.

trap.what: Using the NOR truth table for a NAND latch, or reading a NAND latch's inputs as active-high.
trap.why: The two circuits are duals. The NAND latch is set by a 0 on S' and its forbidden combination is both inputs 0, so every row flips.
trap.counterexample: On a NAND latch with S' = 0 and R' = 1 the output is set to 1, whereas the same numbers on a NOR latch (S = 0, R = 1) reset it to 0.

check.question: Write the next-state value of a NOR SR latch for all four input combinations, assuming Q = 0 before the inputs are applied.
check.answer: S, R = 0, 0 gives Q+ = 0 (hold); 0, 1 gives 0 (reset); 1, 0 gives 1 (set); 1, 1 gives Q = Q' = 0, which is forbidden.
check.explanation: From Q+ = S + R'Q with Q = 0 the term R'Q vanishes, so Q+ = S for the three legal rows. The forbidden row is the one the equation cannot describe.

sources.title: Lecture 7 - Synchronous Sequential Logic
sources.channel: IIT Bombay, CS 226 Digital Logic Design (Ashutosh Trivedi)
sources.note: The complete slide text was served and read: the sequential definition, the synchronous and asynchronous classification, the NOR and NAND SR latch tables, the gated SR latch, the D latch, the problem with latches, the edge-triggered D flip-flop and setup and hold, the JK and T flip-flops with their characteristic equations, the analysis example, the seven-step synthesis procedure, state reduction and the binary, Gray and one-hot assignment table.

sources.title: फ्लिप-फ्लॉप (Flip-flop)
sources.note: The article was read in full and translated into English here. It gives the two stable output states, the latch name, the four kinds (SR, D, T, JK), the T characteristic equation Q_next = T XOR Q, and the combined characteristic and excitation table for D, T, SR and JK. The excitation table is the one place where a Hindi source supplied a table this repository publishes, and the table is recomputed in scripts/validate.py rather than trusted.

sourceLine: Both latch tables, the active-high and active-low reading, the gated version and the forbidden row: IIT Bombay CS 226 Lecture 7 (English, read in full). The characteristic equation Q* = S + R'Q: Auburn ELEC 2200 Lecture 7 (English, read in full). The latch as a two-state memory element: the Hindi Wikipedia article on flip-flops (translated). No verified GATE CSE question of this topic is decided by a bare latch table, which is why this card carries none.

covers: the NOR SR latch solved by iterating its two gate equations
two stable states, and holding as a fixed point rather than an absence of behaviour
S = R = 1 collapses to (0,0): the pair is no longer complementary
the release from S = R = 1 oscillates with period 2: the next state is undefined
